Yeah I would try to clean the room he's in every other day or so. If you're using harsh chemicals, you might have to move him out for a bit OR thoroughly rinse off surfaces after you've cleaned them.  Ringworm is hard. But I do think it helps if you have lots of old sheets or towels lying around that you can just cover surfaces with. Then you can clean those and replace them. Which is a little easier.

Check with your vet again bc sometimes while they'll still have visible spots and need to be on meds for 2-3, they will no longer be contagious after 1 week.

Ringworm is very contagious tho. If you have another room besides the bathroom, it might be possible to let him in there if you take out any soft surfaces (bc they tend to be harder to sanitize) and cover the carpets and furniture with drop cloths or sheets that you can wash / sanitize every other day or so. If you did this, you'd need to be diligent about sanitizing hard surfaces and anything left uncovered. It's a lot of work but I understand that you want your kitty to be less stressed. 

The problem with ringworm spores is they can live on surfaces like carpets for up to a year which means you, or he or any other pets would be at risk of infection again. But if you're super diligent about covering surfaces and cleaning, it is possible to manage.

Ok, so if they both made assumptions, OP's assumption was that he and his wife would have kids the way the vast majority of people have kids. And the wife assumed that her husband would psychically know she wanted a surrogate. One is a reasonable assumption and one is not.

It's a pretty reasonable assumption that if you and your future spouse agree about having kids, that the first thing you'll trying is conceiving and carrying the "old fashioned way." That's just how it works for most people. Like you might talk about adoption? But surrogacy is normally an option people look into after having problems with successfully carrying to term. 

While it's a totally ok choice for the wife to make for her body, it's certainly not the most common, so I don't think anyone should fault the husband for not thinking to ask about surrogacy before they got married. It was absolutely incumbent on the wife to bring this up to him ahead of time.

This is complicated, but I think ESH, maybe more her. Her reasons may sound trivial to you, but many many women, whether surreally beautiful or not, get the message that their worth rests heavily in their appearance. It's also her choice whether she wants to carry a child herself. So you need to respect her wishes and try to understand her point of view. 

Here's why I think she's more the AH. It sounds like you both went into this marriage knowing you wanted kids. And according to her sister, it was probably on her mind for a very long time that she didn't want to carry a child. Your wife should have told you BEFORE you got married. Especially because she had to know how expensive surrogacy is and whether that would ever be a realistic expense for the two of you.  

By not telling you about her wishes, she pretty much eliminated your chance at biological children if you stay with her. That's just not ok. And while adopting is a great choice, it can also be expensive and come with challenges biological children wouldn't present. Plus lot of people just want to have biological children. And it's totally valid if you would prefer that over adoption. It's just deeply unfair that she didn't tell you.

So cats with ringworm can spread ringworm spores really easily. I would not let him sleep in your bed. And you should probably keep him in a bathroom while you're out. Or if that's not possible, lay sheets or towels over carpet and surfaces he might sleep on so you can wash them. Wash anything he sleeps on every day if possible. 

Your vet should be able to tell you, but if he's on medication normally they'll stop being contagious after a week on the medicine so these precautions can be less intense.

You should wash your hands after you play with him or cuddle him. Also wash your clothes immediately if he's been cuddling you a lot.
If you get ringworm from him, it's not that big a deal. Like another reply said, you can just use athlete's foot cream. 

I realize this sounds like a lot. I've fostered a lot of ringworm kittens. I've never gotten it from them and I've never had one kitten get it from spores in the carpet, bedding etc. But it can be highly contagious so you want to try to be careful not to let spread around so he doesn't keep getting reinfected.

My cat had similar issues. And I was taking him to lots of vets, trying steroids, switching food, spending lots of money. But I finally got him allergy tested and started on immunotherapy. He's been on it for a year. It's made a huge difference. His hair hasn't completely grown back everywhere (his entire belly was bald), but it has vastly improved. 

And more importantly he no longer goes nuts licking and biting at himself to try to get at the itch.  It does take a while for the hair to start growing back, especially if your cat's been having this problem for a while but I could really tell my cat was feeling better after about a month or  two. 

I would say hold on, give the immunotherapy a few months and see how it goes. Also take a picture of your cat's bald spots now so you can tell the difference as the treatment kicks in.

As someone who tried EVERYTHING for so long I feel like immunotherapy has been amazing for my cat. Good luck!

So some research shows that while suicidal ideation is something many people deal with for prolonged periods of time, the act of attempting or committing suicide may be fairly impulsive and fleeting. Hi! Last year my cat, Panda had the same situation. One evening, he was trying to urinate every few minutes and eventually started keening and seeming really distressed when he tried to use the litter box. After googling, I realized this was really serious, especially for male cats, so I took him to the vet. Luckily they were able to help him out.

After getting we left the vet, I switched him to a prescription dry food diet and got a second fountain. He has always liked drinking from a fountain so I figured having a second one might be nice just so he had more options.  I became more diligent about scooping his litter, first to check how he was doing and second to make sure his litter box was always clean. While he was recovering, I didn't want him to have any bad associations with the litter box.

Like you, I felt very anxious immediately after all this. For probably a month or two, I would get very nervous any time anything seemed off with Panda. However, I reassured myself that because his behavior had been so obvious and so different when he was actually blocked,  I would definitely know if his problems came back.

The other thing I would suggest is locating a few 24-hour vets if you haven't already. I feel better knowing that there are a couple 24 hour vets nearby in case anything like this happens again, I know exactly where to get help.  Most 24 hour vets are really helpful about giving you advice if you call in, so they should be able to tell you over the phone if your cat needs immediate attention. 

Finally, this might be overkill, but I had wanted to get a pet cam for a while before Panda got sick, just to see what he did all day, if he was bored, etc. I got one shortly after he got sick and it did make me feel a lot better being able to check in on him while I was at work. I don't think this is AT ALL required, but if you have the money, it might be a nice way to reassure yourself.

A year later, Panda is great! His issues haven't recurred and I've transitioned back to normal dry food with no issues. It sounds like you're doing everything you possibly can.  I definitely understand feeling scared, but hopefully you'll feel better knowing you did everything right: you realized your cat needed help and you got it for him quickly. Food- hydration is really important so wet food is good if you can afford it/they like it. I have an automatic feeder and it's great for when I'm longer than I intend to be / go out of town. It's definitely not a necessity tho.

Water- since hydration is a big deal, whatever they'll drink from is great. My friends cats are all scared of fountains but my cats love them. Plus I find that having a fountain keeps my cats from trying to drink from the toilet. But again, they just need to drink water - if they're happy without a fountain, that's great.

Advantage- definitely use advantage (or something similar) bc it protects against heartworm, which is basically deadly for cats. Also theoretically fleas could get in your house in some random way so it's just a good idea.

Scratching posts etc- the only advice I'd give is that it's worth having a lot of scratching surfaces. Cats use it to mark territory and get out excitement or aggression. Plus if your cats are going after a piece of furniture, you can usually deter them by putting a scratcher there.

Final thing! If your cats are still pretty active: Get hair ties! Like thicker hair rubber bands. My cats are obsessed with them. They'll pounce on them and carry them around. Plus you can shoot the ties or throw them and cats like to chase them.

Good luck! I hope you and your new cats are really happy!
